name: Categorical imperative
summary: Kant's supreme principle of morality: an unconditional command of reason, binding on every rational agent whatever their desires, tested by whether one's maxim could be willed as a universal law and by treating humanity always as an end, never merely as a means. Its Kingdom of Ends formula pictures a community of autonomous, self-legislating persons whose laws all could will.
scope: The categorical imperative as Kant sets it out in the Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals and develops in the Critique of Practical Reason and the Metaphysics of Morals, with its formulations (universal law, humanity, autonomy, kingdom of ends) as the encyclopedias and Paton's study present them. Kant himself is left off the key figures (human rights holds him). It covers the principle and what Kant's own texts and the commentators derive from it about persons, duties, law and a community of rational beings. It excludes Kant's wider political philosophy as a separate subject, the Golden Rule and later Kantian or neo-Kantian systems except where the sources tie them to the imperative, and the religious 'categorical imperatives' of unrelated books (Morgan, 1930, a Christian sermon series).
